questions.stem: Per this page, when a task handed to a ForkJoinPool with `execute(task)` throws an exception, where does the caller see it?

options.text: Only if the caller kept the task and later calls join() or get() on it
options.says: The page says execute() returns void, and its exception surfaces only if you keep the task object and call join()/get() on it.

options.text: Right away, because execute() rethrows it to the caller like invoke() does
options.says: The page says only invoke() throws the task's exception to the caller; execute() returns immediately.

options.text: In the pool's shutdown() call, which reports every failure it collected
options.says: The page names join() and get() as where exceptions surface; it gives shutdown() no such role.

questions.stem: Per this page, why should a parallel stream that makes blocking HTTP calls run in a custom ForkJoinPool rather than the common one?

options.text: The common pool rejects tasks that block, so the HTTP calls would raise errors
options.says: The page's problem code runs the blocking call on a common pool thread; the harm it names is saturation, not a refusal.

options.text: The common pool serves the whole JVM, so blocked workers delay other code
options.says: The page calls the common pool a JVM-wide singleton used by parallelStream() and others, and says a custom pool gives isolation.

options.text: The common pool has a single worker, so the HTTP calls would run in turn
options.says: The page says the common pool's default parallelism is availableProcessors() - 1 and can be overridden, so it is not one thread.
